text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt rows with Finance Minister Theo Waigel over budget. The coalition sobered by negotiations with opposition Social Democrats to find compromise on tax reform bill
- The record highs on international markets do not let up. The DAX climbs to 4055 points
- Education Minister Juergen Ruettgers says one training is not enough, that each person needs to learn three professions
- Rudi Geil, new government official responsible for the former eastern Germany, says more should be done for small to medium-sized companies in eastern Germany
- Berlin building workers and employers are close to a pay agreement
HANDELSBLATT
- German shares go from record high to record high. The message of the banks to investors is clear: this is not the time to get out of the German share market.

- The budget deficit grows. The supplementary budget for 1997 was presented by Finance Minister Theo Waigel yesterday to cover 18.7 billion marks. New debt has increased from 53.3 to 71.2 billion marks
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's tax reform bill is not yet dead. Negotiations in mediation committee start today to thrash out compromise with the opposition Social Democrats

- Hans-Olaf Henkel, the president of the German Industry Federation (BDI), calls on President Roman Herzog for a reform of the political system arguing that the currency system puts Germany at a disadvantage when competing with other countries in the world
- Metro invests more abroad. The firm wants to use over a third of its investments worth 1.9 billion marks for its activities in Poland, Turkey and China.
- China is taking part in Expo 2000 trade fair in German city of Hanover to take place for the beginning of millennium. The United States has still not agreed to take part yet
- 4,000 jobs fewer in hard coal mining industry
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- German political parties may exclude members of Scientology if they wish, Bonn court ruled
- Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the BDI German industry federation, calls for debate over the country's political system
- Germany's BND intelligence agency wants cover names for only a few of its spies
- German Constitutional Court upholds guilty verdict of former Stasi colonel Alexander Schalck-Golodkowdki for illegal arms import into former East Germany from the west during the Cold War
- The Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Chistian Democrats, want to introduce a CO2 tax despite opposition from CSU Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber
- Deutsche Telecom will not carry out forced redundancies before the year 2000, saying it would introduce more flexible personnel planning
DIE WELT
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition agree on the 1998 budget
- Fewer big firms in eastern Germany.
- Suspected ETA supporter Renate Heike Schubbert hads herself in to German police
- Privatisation of Duesseldorf airport, a model for other cities?

- Tax talks between ruling coalition and opposition Social Democrats going down a dead end. No swift agreement on the abolition of capital tax for companies in sight. Industry warns government against compromising its aims
- Juergen Schneider, former property tycoon facing charges of fraud, wraps himself in veil of silence
- German hard coal mining industry cuts 7,000 jobs

- Ifo economic research institute shows only 22 percent of firms are prepared to take in more apprentices than the previous year, while 15 percent want to reduce the number of apprenticeship this year
